title: On the possibility of differential algebraic elimination of the spinor field from the Maxwell-Dirac electrodynamics
summary: We investigate whether the spinor field can be eliminated from the Maxwell-Dirac equations by differential algebraic methods. A generic truncated power series solution is constructed, the prolonged system of the Maxwell-Dirac electrodynamics is linearized about the solution, and the ranks of the associated coefficient matrices are computed. The results indicate that, generically, the spinor components are uniquely determined by the electromagnetic field and its derivatives. This strongly suggests that differential-algebraic elimination of the spinor field is possible.

AI.tldr: Differential-algebraic analysis suggests spinor field can be eliminated from Maxwell-Dirac equations, with spinor components uniquely determined by electromagnetic field and its derivatives.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the spinor field can be eliminated from the Maxwell-Dirac equations using differential algebraic methods, potentially simplifying the description of electrodynamics by reducing the number of fundamental fields.
AI.method: Constructed a generic truncated power series solution, linearized the prolonged system of Maxwell-Dirac electrodynamics about this solution, and computed the ranks of associated coefficient matrices to analyze the algebraic dependencies between fields.
AI.result: Results indicate that generically, the spinor components are uniquely determined by the electromagnetic field and its derivatives, suggesting the spinor field is not independent but algebraically dependent on the electromagnetic field.
AI.conclusion: Differential-algebraic elimination of the spinor field from Maxwell-Dirac equations appears possible, which could lead to a reduced formulation of electrodynamics where only the electromagnetic field is fundamental.

title: Experimental Characterization and Model Validation of Interference in Classical-QKD Coexistence Transmission
comment: Submitted for the 2026 Conference on Lasers and Electro-Optic
summary: We present an experimental characterization of coexistence-induced interference in QKD transmission arising from SpRS and FWM, validating a comprehensive semi-analytical model for accurate noise estimation. Experimental results show good agreement with theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: Experimental characterization of coexistence-induced interference in QKD transmission from SpRS and FWM, with validation of semi-analytical noise estimation model.
AI.motivation: To characterize and quantify interference effects in quantum key distribution (QKD) systems when co-existing with classical channels, specifically spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS) and four-wave mixing (FWM) noise sources.
AI.method: Experimental characterization combined with development and validation of a comprehensive semi-analytical model for accurate noise estimation from SpRS and FWM interference.
AI.result: Experimental results show good agreement with theoretical predictions, validating the semi-analytical model's accuracy in estimating coexistence-induced interference in QKD transmission.
AI.conclusion: The validated semi-analytical model provides accurate noise estimation for QKD systems affected by SpRS and FWM interference, enabling better system design and performance optimization in coexistence scenarios.

title: Entanglement-assisted Hamiltonian dynamics learning
comment: Main text: 5 pages, 2 figures. Total text: 9 pages, 4 figures
summary: Approximating the dynamics given by a complex many-body Hamiltonian with a simpler effective model lies at the interface of quantum Hamiltonian learning and quantum simulation. In this context, quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs) have been shown to outperform standard Trotter-based approximations. However, their performance is often hindered by training plateaus and local minima that become increasingly severe with system size. To overcome these limitations, we propose an entanglement-assisted learning strategy that couples a single randomly initialized auxiliary qubit to the learning system at an intermediate stage of the training process. The interplay between randomization and entanglement significantly enhances the learning performance of the protocol.

AI.tldr: Proposes entanglement-assisted learning strategy using auxiliary qubit to enhance QGAN performance for Hamiltonian approximation, overcoming training plateaus and local minima.
AI.motivation: Quantum GANs for Hamiltonian approximation face training plateaus and local minima that worsen with system size, limiting their effectiveness for quantum simulation and Hamiltonian learning tasks.
AI.method: Introduces entanglement-assisted learning strategy: couples single randomly initialized auxiliary qubit to learning system at intermediate training stage, leveraging interplay between randomization and entanglement to enhance learning performance.
AI.result: The proposed approach significantly enhances learning performance of QGANs for Hamiltonian approximation, overcoming limitations of standard training methods.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-assisted learning with auxiliary qubits provides effective strategy to improve QGAN training for quantum Hamiltonian approximation, addressing scalability challenges in quantum simulation.

title: KPZ-like transport in long-range interacting spin chains proximate to integrability
summary: Isotropic integrable spin chains such as the Heisenberg model feature superdiffusive spin transport belonging to an as-yet-unidentified dynamical universality class closely related to that of Kardar, Parisi, and Zhang (KPZ). To determine whether these results extend to more generic one-dimensional models, particularly those realizable in quantum simulators, we investigate spin and energy transport in non-integrable, long-range Heisenberg models using state-of-the-art tensor network methods. Despite the lack of integrability and the asymptotic expectation of diffusion, for power-law models (with exponent $2 < α< \infty$) we observe long-lived $z=3/2$ superdiffusive spin transport and two-point correlators consistent with KPZ scaling functions, up to times $t \sim 10^3/J$. We conjecture that this KPZ-like transport is due to the proximity of such power-law-interacting models to the integrable family of Inozemtsev models, which we show to also exhibit KPZ-like spin transport across all interaction ranges. Finally, we consider anisotropic spin models naturally realized in Rydberg atom arrays and ultracold polar molecules, demonstrating that a wide range of long-lived, non-diffusive transport can be observed in experimental settings.

AI.tldr: Long-range non-integrable Heisenberg models exhibit long-lived KPZ-like superdiffusive spin transport with dynamical exponent z=3/2, despite asymptotic expectation of diffusion, due to proximity to integrable Inozemtsev models.
AI.motivation: To determine whether superdiffusive spin transport observed in isotropic integrable spin chains (like Heisenberg model) extends to more generic one-dimensional models, particularly those realizable in quantum simulators, and to investigate if these results persist in non-integrable, long-range systems.
AI.method: Investigate spin and energy transport in non-integrable, long-range Heisenberg models using state-of-the-art tensor network methods. Study power-law models with exponent 2 < α < ∞, analyze proximity to integrable Inozemtsev models, and consider anisotropic spin models realizable in Rydberg atom arrays and ultracold polar molecules.
AI.result: Despite lack of integrability and asymptotic expectation of diffusion, power-law models exhibit long-lived z=3/2 superdiffusive spin transport up to times t ~ 10³/J, with two-point correlators consistent with KPZ scaling functions. Inozemtsev models also show KPZ-like spin transport across all interaction ranges. Anisotropic spin models demonstrate wide range of long-lived, non-diffusive transport observable in experimental settings.
AI.conclusion: KPZ-like superdiffusive transport extends beyond integrable models to non-integrable, long-range systems, persisting as long-lived phenomena due to proximity to integrable families. This suggests such transport can be observed in experimental quantum simulators using Rydberg atoms and polar molecules.

title: Optimizing p-spin models through hypergraph neural networks and deep reinforcement learning
summary: p-spin glasses, characterized by frustrated many-body interactions beyond the conventional pairwise case (p>2), are prototypical disordered systems whose ground-state search is NP-hard and computationally prohibitive for large instances. Solving this problem is not only fundamental for understanding high-order disorder, structural glasses, and topological phases, but also central to a wide spectrum of hard combinatorial optimization tasks. Despite decades of progress, there still lacks an efficient and scalable solver for generic large-scale p-spin models. Here we introduce PLANCK, a physics-inspired deep reinforcement learning framework built on hypergraph neural networks. PLANCK directly optimizes arbitrary high-order interactions, and systematically exploits gauge symmetry throughout both training and inference. Trained exclusively on small synthetic instances, PLANCK exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to systems orders of magnitude larger, and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art thermal annealing methods across all tested structural topologies and coupling distributions. Moreover, without any modification, PLANCK achieves near-optimal solutions for a broad class of NP-hard combinatorial problems, including random k-XORSAT, hypergraph max-cut, and conventional max-cut. The presented framework provides a physics-inspired algorithmic paradigm that bridges statistical mechanics and reinforcement learning. The symmetry-aware design not only advances the tractable frontiers of high-order disordered systems, but also opens a promising avenue for machine-learning-based solvers to tackle previously intractable combinatorial optimization challenges.

AI.tldr: PLANCK is a physics-inspired deep reinforcement learning framework using hypergraph neural networks to solve large-scale p-spin glass models and NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems with strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: p-spin glasses with frustrated many-body interactions (p>2) are NP-hard problems that are computationally prohibitive for large instances. Solving these problems is fundamental for understanding high-order disorder, structural glasses, topological phases, and combinatorial optimization tasks, but there lacks an efficient and scalable solver for generic large-scale p-spin models.
AI.method: PLANCK uses a physics-inspired deep reinforcement learning framework built on hypergraph neural networks. It directly optimizes arbitrary high-order interactions and systematically exploits gauge symmetry throughout both training and inference. The system is trained exclusively on small synthetic instances.
AI.result: PLANCK exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to systems orders of magnitude larger than training instances, consistently outperforms state-of-the-art thermal annealing methods across all tested structural topologies and coupling distributions, and achieves near-optimal solutions for NP-hard problems including random k-XORSAT, hypergraph max-cut, and conventional max-cut without any modification.
AI.conclusion: PLANCK provides a physics-inspired algorithmic paradigm bridging statistical mechanics and reinforcement learning. The symmetry-aware design advances tractable frontiers of high-order disordered systems and opens a promising avenue for machine-learning-based solvers to tackle previously intractable combinatorial optimization challenges.

title: Limits of Clifford Disentangling in Tensor Network States
summary: Tensor network methods leverage the limited entanglement of quantum states to efficiently simulate many-body systems. Alternatively, Clifford circuits provide a framework for handling highly entangled stabilizer states, which have low magic and are thus also classically tractable. Clifford tensor networks combine the benefits of both approaches, exploiting Clifford circuits to reduce the classical complexity of the tensor network description of states, with promising effects on simulation approaches. We study the disentangling power of Clifford transformations acting on tensor networks, with a particular emphasis on entanglement cooling strategies. We identify regimes where exact or heuristic Clifford disentanglers are effective, explain the link between the two approaches, and characterize their breakdown as non-Clifford resources accumulate. Additionally, we prove that, beyond stabilizer settings, no Clifford operation can universally disentangle even a single qubit from an arbitrary non-Clifford rotation. Our results clarify both the capabilities and fundamental limitations of Clifford-based simulation methods.

AI.tldr: Clifford tensor networks combine tensor network efficiency with Clifford circuit tractability to reduce classical complexity of quantum state simulation, with analysis of disentangling power and fundamental limitations.
AI.motivation: To develop more efficient classical simulation methods for quantum systems by combining tensor network approaches (which exploit limited entanglement) with Clifford circuits (which handle highly entangled stabilizer states efficiently), creating Clifford tensor networks that reduce classical complexity.
AI.method: Study disentangling power of Clifford transformations acting on tensor networks, focusing on entanglement cooling strategies. Analyze regimes where exact or heuristic Clifford disentanglers are effective, explain connections between approaches, and characterize breakdown as non-Clifford resources accumulate.
AI.result: Identified regimes where Clifford disentanglers work effectively, established link between exact and heuristic approaches, characterized breakdown conditions with non-Clifford resource accumulation, and proved fundamental limitation: beyond stabilizer settings, no Clifford operation can universally disentangle even a single qubit from arbitrary non-Clifford rotation.
AI.conclusion: Clifford tensor networks offer promising simulation advantages by reducing classical complexity, but have fundamental limitations - Clifford operations cannot universally disentangle non-Clifford rotations, clarifying both capabilities and boundaries of Clifford-based simulation methods.

title: Enhanced Superconducting Nanowire Single Photon Detector Performances using Silicon Capping
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures; first two listed authors have equal contribution
summary: Niobium Titanium nitride (NbTiN) based superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (SNSPDs) are known for their high performance across a wide spectral range, from the X-ray to the mid-infrared. Nonetheless, fabrication challenges and performance degradation attributable to surface oxidation and lack of uniformity in films thinner than 5 nm remain a significant barrier for achieving high-quality detectors. In this work, we study the influence of a Silicon capping layer on film properties and on the performance of SNSPDs. A Silicon capping layer effectively suppresses oxidation and increases the superconducting transition temperature. This enables superconductivity in films as thin as 3 nm at 3 K, increases critical current in patterned nanowires and significantly extends the saturation plateau from the visible to the near infrared (up to 2050 nm): These detectors maintain sub-50 ps timing jitter, even for nanowires as wide as 250 nm and with detection areas of 20x20μm2. Our results establish that thinner films protected by a capping layer allow for the fabrication of wider wires, decreasing nanofabrication challenges and extending the operating temperature range for efficient single photon detection.

AI.tldr: Silicon capping layer on NbTiN SNSPDs suppresses oxidation, enables superconductivity in 3nm films, improves critical current, extends spectral range to 2050nm, maintains sub-50ps jitter with wider 250nm wires, and reduces fabrication challenges.
AI.motivation: NbTiN-based SNSPDs face fabrication challenges and performance degradation due to surface oxidation and lack of uniformity in films thinner than 5nm, limiting high-quality detector development.
AI.method: Study the influence of a Silicon capping layer on film properties and SNSPD performance. The capping layer suppresses oxidation and increases superconducting transition temperature.
AI.result: Silicon capping enables superconductivity in films as thin as 3nm at 3K, increases critical current in patterned nanowires, extends saturation plateau from visible to near-infrared (up to 2050nm), maintains sub-50ps timing jitter even for 250nm-wide nanowires with 20x20μm² detection areas.
AI.conclusion: Thinner films protected by a capping layer allow fabrication of wider wires, decreasing nanofabrication challenges and extending operating temperature range for efficient single photon detection.

title: Hardware-Agnostic Modeling of Quantum Side-Channel Leakage via Conditional Dynamics and Learning from Full Correlation Data
comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Quantum Control, Computing, and Learning (IEEE qCCL2026)
summary:
We study a sequential coherent side-channel model in which an adversarial probe qubit interacts with a target qubit during a hidden gate sequence. Repeating the same hidden sequence for $N$ shots yields an empirical full-correlation record: the joint histogram $\widehat{P}_g(b)$ over probe bit-strings $b\in\{0,1\}^k$, which is a sufficient statistic for classical post-processing under identically and independently distributed (i.i.d.) shots but grows exponentially with circuit depth. We first describe this sequential probe framework in a coupling- and measurement-agnostic form, emphasizing the scaling of the observation space and why exact analytic distinguishability becomes intractable with circuit depth.
  We then specialize to a representative instantiation (a controlled-rotation probe coupling with fixed projective readout and a commuting $R_x$ gate alphabet) where we (i) derive a depth-dependent leakage envelope whose maximizer predicts a "Goldilocks" coupling band as a function of depth, and (ii) provide an operational decoder, via machine learning, a single parameter-conditioned map from $\widehat{P}_g$ to Alice's per-step gate labels, generalizing across coupling and noise settings without retraining. Experiments over broad coupling and noise grids show that strict sequence recovery concentrates near the predicted coupling band and degrades predictably under decoherence and finite-shot estimation.

AI.tldr: Sequential coherent side-channel attack model using adversarial probe qubit to extract hidden gate sequences via empirical correlation records, with depth-dependent leakage analysis and ML-based operational decoder.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify information leakage in quantum systems through sequential coherent side-channels, where an adversarial probe interacts with target qubits during hidden gate operations, addressing the exponential growth of observation space with circuit depth.
AI.method: Develops a sequential probe framework in coupling- and measurement-agnostic form, then specializes to controlled-rotation probe coupling with projective readout and commuting Rx gate alphabet. Derives depth-dependent leakage envelope and provides ML-based operational decoder mapping empirical correlation records to gate labels.
AI.result: Identifies "Goldilocks" coupling band as function of depth where sequence recovery is optimal, demonstrates ML decoder generalizes across coupling/noise settings without retraining, shows recovery concentrates near predicted coupling band and degrades predictably under decoherence and finite-shot estimation.
AI.conclusion: Sequential coherent side-channels enable extraction of hidden gate sequences with depth-dependent optimal coupling regimes, and ML-based decoders provide practical operational tools for sequence recovery across varying experimental conditions.

title: Dynamic Synaptic Modulation of LMG Qubits populations in a Bio-Inspired Quantum Brain
summary: We present a biologically inspired quantum neural network that encodes neuronal populations as fully connected qubits governed by the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) quantum Hamiltonian and stabilized by a synaptic-efficacy feedback implementing activity-dependent homeostatic control. The framework links collective quantum many-body modes and attractor structure to population homeostasis and rhythmogenesis, outlining scalable computational primitives -- stable set points, controllable oscillations, and size-dependent robustness -- that position LMG-based architectures as promising blueprints for bio-inspired quantum brains on future quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: A quantum neural network using LMG Hamiltonian with homeostatic control links quantum many-body physics to neural population dynamics, enabling stable computational primitives for quantum neuromorphic computing.
AI.motivation: To develop biologically inspired quantum neural networks that bridge quantum many-body physics with neural population dynamics, creating scalable computational primitives for future quantum neuromorphic hardware.
AI.method: Encodes neuronal populations as fully connected qubits governed by the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick quantum Hamiltonian, stabilized by synaptic-efficacy feedback implementing activity-dependent homeostatic control.
AI.result: Links collective quantum many-body modes and attractor structure to population homeostasis and rhythmogenesis, outlining scalable computational primitives including stable set points, controllable oscillations, and size-dependent robustness.
AI.conclusion: LMG-based architectures represent promising blueprints for bio-inspired quantum brains on future quantum hardware, offering a framework that connects quantum physics with neural computation.

title: Benchmarking the Lights Out Problem on Real Quantum Hardware
summary: We implement the Lights Out problem on a 2D grid and on Mobius ladder graphs and evaluate the performance of Grover's search on real quantum hardware. We use two instances using 9 and 16 qubits, and implement them on publicly available quantum hardware by IBM and IQM. Our experiments show improvements in IBM hardware between the Heron r1 and Heron r2 generations, highlighting progress in IBM hardware during the 2023-2024 period. The Lights Out circuits produced output distributions close to uniform on IQM devices. To diagnose device limitations, we additionally ran a small Grover SAT baseline, finding that IQM Garnet performs more reliably than other tested IQM devices. We also observed that QPUs of the same manufacturing revision can differ significantly in performance (a newer device is not guaranteed to be better), and that calibration has a significant impact on the performance of quantum devices, so the choice of device strongly depends on calibration quality.

AI.tldr: Experimental evaluation of Grover's search on quantum hardware using Lights Out problem instances, comparing IBM and IQM devices with performance analysis across different generations and calibrations.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the performance of Grover's search algorithm on real quantum hardware using concrete problem instances (Lights Out), compare different quantum hardware providers (IBM and IQM), and assess hardware improvements over time.
AI.method: Implemented Lights Out problem on 2D grid and Mobius ladder graphs, created quantum circuits for 9 and 16 qubit instances, ran experiments on IBM and IQM quantum hardware, performed comparative analysis including a small Grover SAT baseline for device diagnosis.
AI.result: IBM hardware showed improvements between Heron r1 and r2 generations; IQM devices produced near-uniform output distributions for Lights Out circuits; IQM Garnet performed more reliably than other IQM devices; significant performance variations observed even within same manufacturing revisions; calibration quality strongly impacts device performance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum hardware performance varies significantly between providers and device generations, with calibration quality being a critical factor. IBM showed measurable improvements in their Heron series, while IQM devices demonstrated reliability differences. Device selection should consider calibration status rather than just manufacturing date.

title: Edge-Local and Qubit-Efficient Quantum Graph Learning for the NISQ Era
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a powerful framework for learning representations from graph-structured data, but their direct implementation on near-term quantum hardware remains challenging due to circuit depth, multi-qubit interactions, and qubit scalability constraints. In this work, we introduce a fully quantum graph convolutional architecture designed explicitly for unsupervised learning in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime. Our approach combines a variational quantum feature extraction layer with an edge-local and qubit-efficient quantum message-passing mechanism inspired by the Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA) framework. Unlike prior models that rely on global operations or multi-controlled unitaries, our model decomposes message passing into pairwise interactions along graph edges using only hardware-native single- and two-qubit gates. This design reduces the qubit requirement from $O(Nn)$ to $O(n)$ for a graph with $N$ nodes and $n$-qubit feature registers, enabling implementation on current quantum devices regardless of graph size. We train the model using the Deep Graph Infomax objective to perform unsupervised node representation learning. Experiments on the Cora citation network and a large-scale genomic SNP dataset demonstrate that our model remains competitive with prior quantum and hybrid approaches.

AI.tldr: A quantum graph convolutional architecture for NISQ devices that reduces qubit requirements through edge-local message passing and achieves competitive unsupervised learning performance.
AI.motivation: Direct implementation of GNNs on near-term quantum hardware is challenging due to circuit depth, multi-qubit interactions, and qubit scalability constraints, necessitating NISQ-friendly architectures.
AI.method: Combines variational quantum feature extraction with edge-local quantum message passing using QAOA-inspired pairwise interactions with hardware-native single- and two-qubit gates, reducing qubit requirements from O(Nn) to O(n).
AI.result: The model remains competitive with prior quantum and hybrid approaches on Cora citation network and large-scale genomic SNP dataset using Deep Graph Infomax objective for unsupervised node representation learning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum graph convolutional architecture enables practical implementation of GNNs on current NISQ devices by addressing qubit scalability and circuit depth constraints while maintaining competitive learning performance.

title: Device for MHz-rate rastering of arbitrary 2D optical potentials
summary: Current architectures for neutral-atom arrays utilize devices such as acousto-optic deflectors (AODs) and spatial light modulators (SLMs) to multiplex a single classical control line into N qubit control lines. Dynamic control is speed-limited by the response time of AODs, and geometrically constrained to respect a product structure, limiting motion to row-by-row or column-by-column moves. We propose an optical rastering device that can produce any 2D pattern, not limited to grids, at 1 MHz refresh rates. We demonstrate a design with a resolution of 40 x 40 that can be further scaled up to 100 x 100 to match existing and future neutral atom devices. The ability to simultaneously transport atomic qubits in arbitrary directions will enhance qubit connectivity, enable more efficient circuits, and may have broader applications ranging from LiDAR to fluorescence microscopy.

AI.tldr: Proposes a high-speed optical rastering device for neutral-atom arrays that enables arbitrary 2D pattern generation at 1 MHz refresh rates, overcoming limitations of current AOD/SLM-based architectures.
AI.motivation: Current neutral-atom array architectures using AODs and SLMs have speed limitations (AOD response time) and geometric constraints (product structure limiting motion to row/column moves), restricting qubit connectivity and circuit efficiency.
AI.method: Designs an optical rastering device capable of producing any 2D pattern (not limited to grids) at 1 MHz refresh rates, with demonstrated resolution of 40×40 and scalability to 100×100 to match neutral atom devices.
AI.result: Demonstrates a design achieving 1 MHz refresh rates with 40×40 resolution, scalable to 100×100, enabling simultaneous transport of atomic qubits in arbitrary directions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed device enhances qubit connectivity, enables more efficient quantum circuits, and has broader applications in LiDAR and fluorescence microscopy beyond quantum computing.

title: Multi-emitter oscillating bound states in Waveguide QED
summary: Waveguide quantum electrodynamics platforms have emerged as promising candidates for exploring and implementing non-Markovian quantum phenomena. In this work, we investigate the formation and dynamics of superpositions of bound states in a cavity array waveguide coupled to two spatially separated quantum emitters. By tuning the system parameters, we show that spontaneous emission can drive the system into non-local equilibrium states in which both photonic and emitter populations exhibit persistent oscillations. These states arise from the coexistence of bound states embedded in the energy continuum and bound states outside it, leading to hybrid oscillatory modes. We analytically derive the conditions required for the emergence of these states, numerically simulate their formation through spontaneous emission, and predict their long-time behaviour. Our results demonstrate that such bound-state superpositions enable the generation of emitter-emitter interaction through free evolution, while supporting oscillatory breathing modes of the photon density between the emitters.

AI.tldr: Spontaneous emission in a cavity array waveguide with two quantum emitters can drive the system into non-local equilibrium states with persistent oscillations, enabled by superpositions of bound states both inside and outside the energy continuum.
AI.motivation: To investigate how waveguide quantum electrodynamics platforms can generate and control non-Markovian quantum phenomena, specifically exploring the formation of bound-state superpositions in systems with spatially separated quantum emitters.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of conditions for bound-state superposition emergence, numerical simulation of formation through spontaneous emission, and prediction of long-time behavior in a cavity array waveguide coupled to two quantum emitters.
AI.result: Spontaneous emission drives the system into non-local equilibrium states with persistent oscillations in both photonic and emitter populations, creating hybrid oscillatory modes from coexisting bound states inside and outside the energy continuum.
AI.conclusion: Bound-state superpositions enable emitter-emitter interaction through free evolution while supporting oscillatory breathing modes of photon density between emitters, demonstrating potential for non-Markovian quantum phenomena control.

title: Strong-to-Weak Symmetry Breaking in Open Quantum Systems: From Discrete Particles to Continuum Hydrodynamics
summary: We explore the onset of spontaneous strong-to-weak symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) under U(1)-symmetric (i.e., charge-conserving) open-system dynamics. We define this phenomenon for quantum states and classical probability distributions, and explore it in three complementary models, one of which exhibits nontrivial quantum coherence at short times. Our main conclusions are as follows. In one dimension, the strong symmetry is not spontaneously broken at any finite time; however, correlators probing strong-to-weak symmetry breaking develop order on length scales that grow linearly in time, parametrically faster than charge diffusion. We provide numerical evidence for this scaling in multiple distinct probes of SW-SSB, and derive it from a field-theory analysis. Moreover, we relate this scaling to the problem of inferring the charge inside a subregion by measuring its surroundings, and construct explicit decoding protocols that illustrate its origin. In two dimensions, field theory and numerical simulations support a finite-time Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless-like SW-SSB transition. Within continuum hydrodynamics, by contrast, SW-SSB happens at infinitesimal time in two or more dimensions. The SW-SSB transition time can thus be interpreted as marking the emergence of a continuum hydrodynamic description, or (more precisely) the timescale beyond which non-hydrodynamic information such as discrete particle worldlines can no longer be inferred. We support this picture by analyzing a model in which we exploit SW-SSB to derive a classical stochastic hydrodynamic description from the underlying quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: SW-SSB (spontaneous strong-to-weak symmetry breaking) emerges under U(1)-symmetric open-system dynamics with distinct scaling behaviors: linear growth of order in 1D, finite-time BKT-like transition in 2D, and instantaneous onset in continuum hydrodynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand how spontaneous symmetry breaking transitions from strong to weak forms occur in open quantum systems with U(1) symmetry, and to characterize the timescales and spatial scaling of this phenomenon across different dimensions.
AI.method: Analyzed SW-SSB in three complementary models (including one with quantum coherence), using numerical simulations, field-theory analysis, decoding protocols for charge inference, and continuum hydrodynamic descriptions to study scaling behaviors in 1D and 2D.
AI.result: In 1D, SW-SSB doesn't occur at finite times but correlators develop order with length scales growing linearly in time (faster than charge diffusion). In 2D, evidence supports finite-time BKT-like SW-SSB transition. Continuum hydrodynamics predicts instantaneous SW-SSB in ≥2D.
AI.conclusion: SW-SSB transition time marks emergence of continuum hydrodynamic description, representing timescale beyond which non-hydrodynamic information (discrete particle worldlines) becomes irretrievable, with distinct dimensional scaling behaviors.

title: Contractivity of time-dependent driven-dissipative systems
summary: In a number of physically relevant contexts, a quantum system interacting with a decohering environment is simultaneously subjected to time-dependent controls and its dynamics is thus described by a time-dependent Lindblad master equation. Of particular interest in such systems is to understand the circumstances in which, despite the ability to apply time-dependent controls, they lose information about their initial state exponentially with time i.e., their dynamics are exponentially contractive. While there exists an extensive framework to study contractivity for time-independent Lindbladians, their time-dependent counterparts are far less well understood. In this paper, we study the contractivity of Lindbladians, which have a fixed dissipator (describing the interaction with an environment), but with a time-dependent driving Hamiltonian. We establish exponential contractivity in the limit of sufficiently small or sufficiently slow drives together with explicit examples showing that, even when the fixed dissipator is exponentially contractive by itself, a sufficiently large or a sufficiently fast Hamiltonian can result in non-contractive dynamics. Furthermore, we provide a number of sufficient conditions on the fixed dissipator that imply exponential contractivity independently of the Hamiltonian. These sufficient conditions allow us to completely characterize Hamiltonian-independent contractivity for unital dissipators and for two-level systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies exponential contractivity in quantum systems with time-dependent Lindblad dynamics, focusing on systems with fixed dissipators but time-dependent Hamiltonian drives, establishing conditions for contractivity and showing how large/fast Hamiltonians can disrupt it.
AI.motivation: To understand when quantum systems subjected to both decohering environments (fixed dissipators) and time-dependent controls (Hamiltonian drives) lose information about their initial state exponentially with time, extending contractivity analysis from time-independent to time-dependent Lindbladians.
AI.method: Analyzes contractivity of Lindbladians with fixed dissipators but time-dependent Hamiltonian drives, establishing conditions for exponential contractivity in limits of small/slow drives, providing counterexamples showing how large/fast Hamiltonians can cause non-contractive dynamics, and deriving sufficient conditions on dissipators for Hamiltonian-independent contractivity.
AI.result: Proves exponential contractivity in limits of sufficiently small or sufficiently slow Hamiltonian drives, provides explicit examples showing that even contractive fixed dissipators can become non-contractive with sufficiently large/fast Hamiltonians, and establishes sufficient conditions on fixed dissipators for Hamiltonian-independent contractivity, completely characterizing this for unital dissipators and two-level systems.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent Hamiltonian drives can significantly affect contractivity properties of Lindblad dynamics, with contractivity guaranteed only under certain conditions on drive magnitude/speed or specific dissipator properties, providing a framework for understanding when quantum systems maintain exponential information loss despite time-dependent controls.

title: Lie-Algebraic Analysis of Generators: Approximation-Error Bounds and Barren-Plateau Heuristics
summary: Lie algebras provide a useful framework for theoretical analysis in quantum machine learning, particularly in hybrid quantum-classical learning. From the viewpoint of function approximation, expectation values of parameterized quantum circuits can be viewed as trigonometric polynomials whose accessible Fourier modes are determined by the spectra of the generators. In this study, we describe: (1) a minimax lower bound on the $ L^{2} $-approximation error over a Sobolev ball when the circuit's effective frequency set is contained in a radius-$K$ ball, which yields a scaling law of the form $ Ω(K^{\frac{d}{2} - r}) $ for $ r > \frac{d}{2} $ (assuming the target function belongs to the Sobolev space $ W_2^{r}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) $), and we also derive a Jackson-type upper bound on the approximation error of quantum circuits under Sobolev regularity of the target function, expressed in terms of an effective bandwidth determined by generator spectral gaps; (2) a generator-selection rule motivated by enlarging the effective frequency set via non-commuting generators; and (3) a simple heuristic metric based on the trace component of generators, aimed at characterizing training behaviors related to barren plateaus. Simulation experiments on toy problems illustrate the practical implications of the frequency-spectrum perspective and the proposed heuristics.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes approximation error bounds for parameterized quantum circuits using Lie algebra framework, derives generator selection rules to expand frequency sets, and proposes metrics to characterize barren plateau behaviors.
AI.motivation: To provide theoretical analysis of quantum machine learning using Lie algebras, particularly for understanding function approximation capabilities of parameterized quantum circuits and addressing issues like limited frequency sets and barren plateaus.
AI.method: Uses Lie algebra framework to view quantum circuit expectation values as trigonometric polynomials; derives minimax lower bounds and Jackson-type upper bounds on L²-approximation error; proposes generator selection rules based on non-commuting generators to enlarge effective frequency sets; develops heuristic metric based on trace component of generators to characterize barren plateaus.
AI.result: Established scaling law Ω(K^{d/2 - r}) for minimax lower bound when effective frequency set is in radius-K ball; derived Jackson-type upper bound in terms of effective bandwidth; proposed generator selection rules and trace-based metric; validated through simulation experiments on toy problems.
AI.conclusion: Lie algebra framework provides useful theoretical tools for analyzing quantum machine learning; frequency-spectrum perspective offers insights into approximation capabilities and training behaviors; proposed heuristics can guide generator selection and help characterize barren plateaus in practical quantum circuits.

title: Local and Multi-Scale Strategies to Mitigate Exponential Concentration in Quantum Kernels
summary:
Fidelity-based quantum kernels provide a direct interface between quantum feature maps and classical kernel methods, but they can exhibit exponential concentration: with increasing system size or circuit expressivity, the Gram matrix approaches the identity and suppresses informative similarity structure. We present an empirical study of two mitigation strategies implemented in Qiskit: (i) local (patch-wise) kernels that aggregate subsystem similarities, and (ii) multi-scale kernels that mix local and global similarity across patch granularities.
  We benchmark baseline, local, and multi-scale kernels under matched preprocessing, splits, and SVM protocols on several tabular datasets, sweeping the feature dimension $d\in\{4,6,\dots,20\}$. We report concentration diagnostics based on off-diagonal kernel statistics, spectral richness via effective rank, and centered alignment with labels. Across datasets, local and multi-scale constructions consistently mitigate concentration and yield richer kernel spectra relative to the global fidelity baseline, while the impact on classification accuracy depends on the dataset and dimension.

AI.tldr: Empirical study of two Qiskit-implemented strategies (local patch-wise and multi-scale kernels) to mitigate exponential concentration in fidelity-based quantum kernels, showing improved kernel statistics but mixed classification accuracy results.
AI.motivation: Fidelity-based quantum kernels suffer from exponential concentration where Gram matrices approach identity with increasing system size/circuit expressivity, suppressing informative similarity structure needed for effective kernel methods.
AI.method: Benchmark baseline (global fidelity), local (patch-wise aggregation), and multi-scale (mixing local and global) kernels under matched preprocessing, splits, and SVM protocols across tabular datasets with feature dimensions d∈{4,6,...,20}. Use concentration diagnostics: off-diagonal kernel statistics, spectral richness via effective rank, and centered alignment with labels.
AI.result: Local and multi-scale constructions consistently mitigate concentration and yield richer kernel spectra relative to global fidelity baseline across datasets. Impact on classification accuracy depends on dataset and dimension.
AI.conclusion: Patch-based approaches (local and multi-scale) effectively address exponential concentration in quantum kernels, improving kernel quality metrics, though classification performance improvements are dataset-dependent.

title: Reductions of QAOA Induced by Classical Symmetries: Theoretical Insights and Practical Implications
summary:
The performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is closely tied to the structure of the dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) generated by its Hamiltonians, which determines both its expressivity and trainability. In this work, we show that classical symmetries can be systematically exploited as a design principle for QAOA. Focusing on the MaxCut problem with global bit-flip symmetry, we analyze reduced QAOA instances obtained by fixing a single variable and study how this choice affects the associated DLAs. We show that the structure of the DLAs can change dramatically depending on which variable is held fixed. In particular, we construct explicit examples where the dimension collapses from exponential to quadratic, uncovering phenomena that do not appear in the original formulation.
  Numerical experiments on asymmetric graphs indicate that such reductions often produce DLAs of much smaller dimension, suggesting improved trainability. We also prove that any graph can be embedded into a slightly larger one (requiring only quadratic overhead) such that the standard reduced DLA coincides with the free reduced DLA, in most cases implying exponential dimension and irreducibility on the Hilbert space for reduced QAOA instances. These results establish symmetry-aware reduction as a principled tool for designing expressive and potentially trainable QAOA circuits.

AI.tldr: QAOA performance depends on dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) structure; classical symmetries can be exploited to design QAOA circuits. Fixing variables in MaxCut reduces DLA dimensions, improving trainability while maintaining expressivity.
AI.motivation: The performance of QAOA is tied to the structure of its dynamical Lie algebra, which affects both expressivity and trainability. The paper aims to systematically exploit classical symmetries as a design principle for QAOA to improve these properties.
AI.method: Focus on MaxCut problem with global bit-flip symmetry. Analyze reduced QAOA instances by fixing single variables and study how this affects associated DLAs. Construct explicit examples showing DLA dimension changes. Perform numerical experiments on asymmetric graphs and prove embedding results for graph transformations.
AI.result: DLA structure changes dramatically depending on which variable is fixed, with dimensions collapsing from exponential to quadratic in some cases. Numerical experiments show reduced DLAs often have much smaller dimensions, suggesting improved trainability. Proved any graph can be embedded into a slightly larger one with quadratic overhead such that standard reduced DLA coincides with free reduced DLA, typically implying exponential dimension and irreducibility.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-aware reduction establishes a principled tool for designing expressive and potentially trainable QAOA circuits by exploiting classical symmetries to control DLA structure and dimensions.

title: Reinforcement learning for path integrals in quantum statistical physics
summary: Machine learning is rapidly finding its way into the field of computational quantum physics. One of the most popular and widely studied approaches in this direction is to use neural networks to model quantum states (NQS) in the Hamiltonian formulation of quantum mechanics. However, an alternative angle of attack to leverage machine learning in physics is through the path integral formulation, which has so far received far more limited attention. In this paper, we explore how reinforcement learning can be used to compute a class of Euclidean path integrals that yield the thermal density matrix of a quantum system, thereby enabling the computation of the free energy or other thermal expectation values. In particular, we propose a two-step approach with the unique feature that after a variational approximation for a quantity is obtained in a first step, it can then be used to efficiently compute the exact result in a second step. We benchmark this method on several simple systems and then apply it to the quantum rotor chain.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning approach for computing Euclidean path integrals to obtain thermal density matrix, enabling free energy and thermal expectation value calculations.
AI.motivation: While neural network quantum states (NQS) are popular in Hamiltonian formulation, the path integral formulation has received limited attention for machine learning applications in quantum physics. This paper explores using reinforcement learning to compute Euclidean path integrals for thermal properties.
AI.method: Two-step reinforcement learning approach: first obtains variational approximation, then uses it to efficiently compute exact results. Applied to Euclidean path integrals that yield thermal density matrix.
AI.result: Method benchmarked on several simple systems and applied to quantum rotor chain, demonstrating effectiveness for computing free energy and thermal expectation values.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning provides a viable alternative to NQS approaches for path integral formulations, enabling efficient computation of thermal quantum properties through a two-step variational-exact calculation scheme.

title: Squeezed superradiant lasing of a quantum many-body emitter
summary: In conventional lasers, the emitters are typically incoherent, radiating photons independently; in superradiant lasers, many coherent emitters radiate photons collectively, but they essentially do not interact with each other. Here, we present the concept of quantum many-body lasers, in which the emitters interact coherently and radiate collectively. In this proof-of-concept study, we consider a cavity coupled to many pumped spin-1/2 emitters with all-to-all interaction. We find that the squeezing induced by the coherent many-body interaction can be transferred from the spins to photons through superradiant lasing. This work illustrates the concept of using a pumped quantum many-body system to generate bright quantum light with quantum correlations beyond conventional optical coherence, which can facilitate quantum technologies and the study of nonlinear optics in the quantum realm.

AI.tldr: Quantum many-body lasers use interacting emitters to generate squeezed light beyond conventional lasers.
AI.motivation: To go beyond conventional lasers (incoherent emitters) and superradiant lasers (non-interacting coherent emitters) by creating lasers where emitters interact coherently while radiating collectively.
AI.method: Proof-of-concept study using a cavity coupled to many pumped spin-1/2 emitters with all-to-all interactions, analyzing how squeezing from coherent many-body interactions transfers to photons via superradiant lasing.
AI.result: Squeezing induced by coherent many-body interactions can be transferred from spins to photons through superradiant lasing, generating bright quantum light with quantum correlations beyond conventional optical coherence.
AI.conclusion: Quantum many-body lasers represent a new concept for generating quantum light with enhanced correlations, potentially advancing quantum technologies and enabling study of nonlinear optics in the quantum regime.

title: Structured Unitary Tensor Network Representations for Circuit-Efficient Quantum Data Encoding
summary: Encoding classical data into quantum states is a central bottleneck in quantum machine learning: many widely used encodings are circuit-inefficient, requiring deep circuits and substantial quantum resources, which limits scalability on quantum hardware. In this work, we propose TNQE, a circuit-efficient quantum data encoding framework built on structured unitary tensor network (TN) representations. TNQE first represents each classical input via a TN decomposition and then compiles the resulting tensor cores into an encoding circuit through two complementary core-to-circuit strategies. To make this compilation trainable while respecting the unitary nature of quantum operations, we introduce a unitary-aware constraint that parameterizes TN cores as learnable block unitaries, enabling them to be directly optimized and directly encoded as quantum operators. The proposed TNQE framework enables explicit control over circuit depth and qubit resources, allowing the construction of shallow, resource-efficient circuits. Across a range of benchmarks, TNQE achieves encoding circuits as shallow as $0.04\times$ the depth of amplitude encoding, while naturally scaling to high-resolution images ($256 \times 256$) and demonstrating practical feasibility on real quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: TNQE is a circuit-efficient quantum data encoding framework using structured unitary tensor networks to create shallow encoding circuits for classical data.
AI.motivation: Current quantum data encoding methods are circuit-inefficient, requiring deep circuits and substantial quantum resources, which limits scalability on quantum hardware.
AI.method: TNQE represents classical inputs via tensor network decomposition, then compiles tensor cores into encoding circuits using two complementary core-to-circuit strategies with unitary-aware constraints that parameterize TN cores as learnable block unitaries.
AI.result: TNQE achieves encoding circuits as shallow as 0.04× the depth of amplitude encoding, scales to high-resolution images (256×256), and demonstrates practical feasibility on real quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: TNQE provides a circuit-efficient quantum data encoding framework with explicit control over circuit depth and qubit resources, enabling practical quantum machine learning applications on current hardware.

title: Tomographically-nonlocal entanglement
summary: Entanglement is a central and subtle feature of quantum theory, whose structure and operational behavior can change dramatically when additional physical constraints, such as symmetries or superselection rules, are imposed. Such constraints can give rise to striking and counter-intuitive phenomena, including local broadcasting of entangled states and failures of entanglement monogamy. These effects naturally arise in tomographically nonlocal theories (like real quantum theory, twirled worlds, or fermionic quantum theory), where composite systems possess holistic degrees of freedom that are inaccessible to local measurements. In this work, we study entanglement in such theories within the framework of generalized probabilistic theories. We show that the failure of tomographic locality leads to two qualitatively distinct forms of entanglement, which we term $\textit{tomographically-local}$ entanglement and $\textit{tomographically-nonlocal}$ entanglement. We analyze the operational consequences of this distinction, proving that tomographically-nonlocal entanglement is useless for Bell nonlocality, steering, and teleportation, but sufficient for dense coding and perfectly secure data hiding. This framework clarifies the origin of several previously puzzling features of entanglement that arise when tomographic locality fails, as can happen even in quantum theory when one considers fermions or fundamental superselection rules.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes two types of entanglement in tomographically nonlocal theories: tomographically-local entanglement (useful for Bell nonlocality, steering, teleportation) and tomographically-nonlocal entanglement (useless for those but sufficient for dense coding and secure data hiding).
AI.motivation: To understand how entanglement structure changes under physical constraints like symmetries or superselection rules, which lead to tomographic nonlocality and puzzling phenomena like local broadcasting and failures of entanglement monogamy.
AI.method: Study entanglement in tomographically nonlocal theories within the framework of generalized probabilistic theories, distinguishing two qualitatively different forms of entanglement based on their operational properties.
AI.result: Tomographically-nonlocal entanglement is useless for Bell nonlocality, steering, and teleportation, but sufficient for dense coding and perfectly secure data hiding, while tomographically-local entanglement retains standard quantum entanglement properties.
AI.conclusion: The framework clarifies puzzling features of entanglement in tomographically nonlocal theories (like real quantum theory, fermionic quantum theory) by distinguishing two operationally distinct forms of entanglement with different resource-theoretic properties.

title: What Kind of World Supports Darwinian Evolution? Quantum Foundational Options
summary: Darwinian evolution requires (i) heritable records, (ii) repeatable copying with variation, and (iii) routine irreversibility. Categorical quantum mechanics (CQM) makes precise why ``copy'' and ``delete'' are not generic quantum operations: they exist only for a realized \emph{classical data} sector (a preferred basis/observable; a commutative structure). Decoherence explains how a pointer basis can be selected dynamically, but it does not by itself select a unique outcome. This motivates a neutral presentation of the main ontological options (unique-history, decohered multiplicity, agent-relative facticity, and a stochastic foundation with variable diffusion). We also note the relevance of the ``agency constraint'' argued by Adlam-McQueen-Waegell: in a strictly coherent, basis-unselected ``purely quantum'' regime, minimal agency fails due to no-cloning and linearity, which sharpens the role of classical resources for record-based processes. Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios then serve as a stress test, since they treat ``friends'' simultaneously as coherent quantum systems and as agents possessing stable records. Finally, a stochastic-mechanics foundation (with variable diffusion) offers a continuous bridge between quantum and classical regimes, and suggests a principled way to implement measurement update as conditioning plus a time-symmetric minimal-change rule.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how Darwinian evolution principles require classical records and copying mechanisms, which quantum mechanics lacks due to no-cloning, and explores ontological options for bridging quantum and classical regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand how Darwinian evolution's requirements (heritable records, repeatable copying with variation, routine irreversibility) conflict with quantum mechanics' no-cloning theorem and lack of classical data sectors, and to explore ontological frameworks that can reconcile quantum foundations with evolutionary processes.
AI.method: Uses categorical quantum mechanics (CQM) to analyze why copy and delete operations are not generic in quantum mechanics, examines decoherence's limitations in selecting unique outcomes, presents ontological options (unique-history, decohered multiplicity, agent-relative facticity, stochastic foundation), applies agency constraint analysis, and uses Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios as stress tests.
AI.result: CQM shows copy/delete operations exist only for classical data sectors; decoherence selects pointer basis but not unique outcomes; agency constraint reveals minimal agency fails in purely quantum regimes; stochastic mechanics offers continuous quantum-classical bridge with measurement update as conditioning plus time-symmetric minimal-change rule.
AI.conclusion: Classical resources are essential for record-based evolutionary processes; stochastic mechanics with variable diffusion provides a principled foundation for measurement updates and bridges quantum and classical regimes, addressing fundamental conflicts between quantum mechanics and Darwinian evolution requirements.

title: A resolution of the Ito-Stratonovich debate in quantum stochastic processes
summary: Quantum stochastic processes are widely used in describing open quantum systems and in the context of quantum foundations. Physically relevant quantum stochastic processes driven by multiplicative colored noise are generically non-Markovian and analytically intractable. Further, their Markovian limits are generically inequivalent when using either the Ito or Stratonovich conventions for the same quantum stochastic processes. We introduce a quantum noise homogenization scheme that temporally coarse-grains non-Markovian, colored-noise driven quantum stochastic processes and connects them to their effective white-noise (Markovian) limits. Our approach uses a novel phase-space augmentation that maps the non-Markovian dynamics into a higher dimensional Markovian system and then applies a controlled perturbative coarse-graining scheme in the characteristic time scales of the noise. This allows an explicit analytical algorithm to derive effective Markovian generators with renormalized coefficients and enables imposing various physical constraints on them. We thus resolve the Ito-Stratonovich ambiguity for multiplicative colored noise driven quantum stochastic processes, wherein we show that their consistent Markovian limit corresponds to the Stratonovich convention with renormalized coefficients as well as Ito correction terms. By assuming their Markovian limit unravels completely positive, trace-preserving maps, we further characterize a physically relevant family of non-Markovian quantum stochastic processes driven by multiplicative colored noise.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum noise homogenization scheme that coarse-grains colored-noise driven non-Markovian quantum stochastic processes to their effective white-noise Markovian limits, resolving Ito-Stratonovich ambiguity and enabling derivation of renormalized Markovian generators.
AI.motivation: Quantum stochastic processes driven by multiplicative colored noise are generically non-Markovian and analytically intractable, with their Markovian limits being ambiguous between Ito and Stratonovich conventions. There's a need for systematic methods to connect non-Markovian colored-noise processes to their effective Markovian limits while resolving convention ambiguities.
AI.method: Develops a quantum noise homogenization scheme using phase-space augmentation to map non-Markovian dynamics into higher-dimensional Markovian systems, then applies controlled perturbative coarse-graining in noise characteristic time scales to derive effective Markovian generators with renormalized coefficients.
AI.result: The approach provides an explicit analytical algorithm to derive effective Markovian generators, resolves Ito-Stratonovich ambiguity by showing consistent Markovian limits correspond to Stratonovich convention with renormalized coefficients plus Ito correction terms, and characterizes physically relevant families of non-Markovian quantum stochastic processes.
AI.conclusion: The quantum noise homogenization scheme successfully connects non-Markovian colored-noise driven quantum stochastic processes to their Markovian limits, resolves long-standing convention ambiguities, and provides a systematic framework for analyzing such processes while imposing physical constraints like complete positivity and trace preservation.

title: Quantum-enhanced sensing via spectral noise reduction
summary: We report a direct demonstration of quantum-enhanced sensing in the Fourier domain by comparing single- and two-photon interference in a fiber-based interferometer under strictly identical noise conditions. The simultaneous acquisition of both signals provides a common-mode reference that enables a fair and unambiguous benchmark of quantum advantage. Spectral analysis of the interferometric outputs reveals that quantum correlations do not increase the amplitude of the modulation peak, but instead lower the associated noise floor, resulting in the expected 3 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. This enhancement persists in the sub-shot-noise regime, where the classical signal becomes buried in the spectral background while the two-photon contribution remains resolvable. These observations establish Fourier-domain quantum super-sensitivity as an operational and broadly applicable resource for precision interferometric sensing.

AI.tldr: Direct demonstration of quantum-enhanced sensing in Fourier domain using single- vs two-photon interference in fiber interferometer under identical noise conditions, showing 3 dB SNR improvement through noise floor reduction rather than signal amplitude increase.
AI.motivation: To provide an unambiguous benchmark of quantum advantage in sensing by comparing single- and two-photon interference under strictly identical noise conditions, establishing Fourier-domain quantum super-sensitivity as an operational resource.
AI.method: Simultaneous acquisition of single- and two-photon interference signals in a fiber-based interferometer, using common-mode reference for fair comparison. Spectral analysis of interferometric outputs to examine modulation peaks and noise floors.
AI.result: Quantum correlations lower the noise floor rather than increase modulation amplitude, resulting in 3 dB SNR improvement. Enhancement persists in sub-shot-noise regime where classical signal becomes buried while two-photon contribution remains resolvable.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-domain quantum super-sensitivity is established as an operational and broadly applicable resource for precision interferometric sensing, with quantum advantage demonstrated through noise reduction rather than signal amplification.

title: A Formal Theory for Finite-Dimensional Possibilistic Quantum Mechanics
summary: In this work, we present a logical formalism for reasoning about quantum systems in finite dimension. Contrary to the usual approach in quantum logic, our formalism is based classical first-order logic, which allows us to use the tools of model theory in our study. In particular, we show that our formal theory is complete, meaning that it entirely determines the behaviour of quantum systems. Moreover, we provide a characterization of the models of our formal theory, thus providing new insights in the study of hidden variable models of quantum theory.

AI.tldr: A classical first-order logical formalism for reasoning about quantum systems in finite dimensions, with completeness and model characterization.
AI.motivation: To develop a logical framework for quantum systems based on classical first-order logic rather than traditional quantum logic, enabling the use of model theory tools and providing insights into hidden variable models.
AI.method: Constructs a formal theory using classical first-order logic to describe quantum systems in finite dimensions, applying model theory techniques to analyze the formalism.
AI.result: The formal theory is proven complete (entirely determines quantum system behavior) and provides characterization of its models, offering new insights into hidden variable models of quantum theory.
AI.conclusion: The classical first-order logic approach provides a complete and well-characterized logical formalism for quantum systems, offering advantages over traditional quantum logic and new perspectives on hidden variable theories.

title: Why the Casimir Force for Magnetic Metals Computed by the Lifshitz Theory Using the Drude Model Disagrees with the Measurement Data
summary: We consider the Casimir force in configurations with magnetic metal plates and analyze the reasons why the predictions of the Lifshitz theory using the dielectric permittivity of the Drude model are inconsistent with the measurement data. For this purpose, the contributions of the electromagnetic waves with the transverse magnetic and transverse electric polarizations to the Casimir force are computed using the Lifshitz theory expressed in terms of the pure imaginary Matsubara frequencies. Furthermore, the fractions of the evanescent and propagating waves in these contributions are found using an equivalent formulation of the Lifshitz theory along the real frequency axis. All computations are performed for Au-Ni and Ni-Ni plates using the Drude model and the experimentally consistent plasma model over the separation region from 0.5 to 6~mum, where the total force value is determined by conduction electrons. It is shown that the transverse magnetic contribution to the Casimir force does not depend on the used model of the dielectric permittivity, so that the total difference between the predictions of the Lifshitz theory using the Drude model and the measurement data is determined by the transverse electric contribution. In doing so, as opposed to the case of nonmagnetic metals, both fractions of the evanescent and propagating waves in this contribution depend on the model of the dielectric permittivity used in computations, whereas the magnetic properties of the plate metal influence the Casimir force solely through the fraction of propagating waves in the transverse electric contribution. The issue of a more adequate theoretical description of the electromagnetic response of magnetic metals is discussed.

AI.tldr: Analysis of Casimir force in magnetic metal plates reveals that transverse magnetic contribution is model-independent, while transverse electric contribution causes discrepancies between Drude model predictions and experimental data, with magnetic properties affecting only propagating waves in TE contribution.
AI.motivation: To understand why Lifshitz theory predictions using Drude model dielectric permittivity for magnetic metal plates are inconsistent with measurement data, and to analyze the contributions of different electromagnetic wave polarizations and propagation modes to the Casimir force.
AI.method: Computed contributions of transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE) polarizations to Casimir force using Lifshitz theory expressed in terms of imaginary Matsubara frequencies. Analyzed fractions of evanescent and propagating waves using equivalent formulation along real frequency axis. Performed computations for Au-Ni and Ni-Ni plates using Drude model and plasma model over 0.5-6 μm separation range.
AI.result: TM contribution to Casimir force does not depend on dielectric permittivity model, while total difference between Drude model predictions and measurement data is determined by TE contribution. For magnetic metals, both evanescent and propagating wave fractions in TE contribution depend on dielectric model, with magnetic properties influencing Casimir force only through propagating wave fraction in TE contribution.
AI.conclusion: The discrepancy between Lifshitz theory predictions using Drude model and experimental data for magnetic metal plates originates from the TE polarization contribution, highlighting the need for more adequate theoretical description of electromagnetic response in magnetic metals.

title: Solving the Mysteries of Quantum Mechanics: Why Nature Abhors a Continuum
comment: Proceedings of the Royal Society A. In review
summary: Feynman famously asserted that interference is the only real mystery in quantum mechanics (QM). It is concluded that the reason for this mystery, and thereby the related mysteries of complementarity, non-commutativity of observables, the uncertainty principle and violation of Bell's equality, is that the axioms of QM depend vitally on the continuum nature of Hilbert Space, deemed unphysical. We develop a theory of quantum physics - Rational Quantum Mechanics (RaQM) - in which Hilbert Space is gravitationally discretised. The key to solving the mysteries of QM in RaQM is a number-theoretic property of the cosine function, concealed in QM when angles range over the continuum. This number-theoretic property describes mathematically the utter indivisibility of the quantum world and implies that the laws of physics are profoundly holistic. We contrast holism with nonlocality. In theories which embrace the continuum, the violation of Bell's inequality requires the laws of physics to be either nonlocal or not realistic; both incomprehensible concepts. By contrast, holism, as embodied in Mach's Principle or in the fractal geometry of a chaotic attractor, is neither incomprehensible nor unphysical. As part of this, we solve the deepest mystery of all; why nature makes use of complex numbers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Rational Quantum Mechanics (RaQM), which discretizes Hilbert space gravitationally to resolve quantum mysteries like interference, complementarity, and Bell inequality violations through number-theoretic properties of the cosine function, revealing quantum holism rather than nonlocality.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to resolve fundamental mysteries in quantum mechanics identified by Feynman (interference as the core mystery) and related issues including complementarity, non-commutativity, uncertainty principle, and Bell inequality violations. The authors argue these stem from the unphysical continuum nature of Hilbert space in standard QM.
AI.method: The method involves developing Rational Quantum Mechanics (RaQM) where Hilbert space is gravitationally discretized. The key insight leverages number-theoretic properties of the cosine function that are concealed when angles range over the continuum. This approach reveals quantum holism as distinct from nonlocality.
AI.result: RaQM provides a framework where quantum mysteries are resolved through gravitational discretization of Hilbert space. The number-theoretic properties of cosine mathematically describe quantum indivisibility and imply holistic physical laws. The theory distinguishes holism from nonlocality and explains nature's use of complex numbers.
AI.conclusion: The continuum assumption in standard QM creates unnecessary mysteries. By discretizing Hilbert space gravitationally, RaQM resolves quantum mysteries through number-theoretic properties, revealing quantum holism as a comprehensible physical principle distinct from nonlocality, and explains the fundamental role of complex numbers in nature.

title: Enhancing delocalization and entanglement in asymmetric discrete-time quantum walks
summary: In this paper, we investigate the enhancement of delocalization and coin-position entanglement in asymmetric discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs). The asymmetry results from asymmetric coin operations, asymmetric initial states, and asymmetric polarization-dependent losses. By varying these asymmetry factors, the inverse participation ratio and entanglement entropy of the walker are numerically calculated for different coin and loss parameters, both for symmetric and asymmetric initial states. We then experimentally implement a 16-step asymmetric DTQW using a time-multiplexing fiber loop structure. By choosing an asymmetric initial state, both coin-position entanglement and delocalization are simultaneously enhanced under specific coin parameters. Moreover, we observe that with finite asymmetric polarization-dependent loss, the photon probability on the left side decreases significantly, while that on the right side increases and becomes more localized. Interestingly, under specific coin parameters, the entanglement and delocalization exhibit improved robustness against polarization-dependent loss. These results demonstrate that the DTQWs constitute an ideal platform for investigating photonic delocalization and hybrid entanglement.

AI.tldr: Asymmetric discrete-time quantum walks enhance delocalization and coin-position entanglement through asymmetric coin operations, initial states, and polarization-dependent losses, with experimental demonstration showing improved robustness against losses.
AI.motivation: To investigate how asymmetry in discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) - through asymmetric coin operations, initial states, and polarization-dependent losses - can enhance delocalization and coin-position entanglement, and to experimentally demonstrate these effects.
AI.method: Numerical calculation of inverse participation ratio and entanglement entropy for various asymmetry factors, followed by experimental implementation of a 16-step asymmetric DTQW using a time-multiplexing fiber loop structure with asymmetric initial states and polarization-dependent losses.
AI.result: Simultaneous enhancement of coin-position entanglement and delocalization under specific coin parameters with asymmetric initial states; asymmetric polarization-dependent loss causes left-side photon probability decrease and right-side localization increase; entanglement and delocalization show improved robustness against polarization-dependent loss under specific conditions.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric DTQWs provide an ideal platform for studying photonic delocalization and hybrid entanglement, with demonstrated capability to enhance both properties simultaneously and show improved robustness against losses through strategic asymmetry engineering.

title: Measurement Induced Subradiance
summary: Preparing subradiant steady states of collectively emitting quantum two-level emitters (TLEs) is hindered by their dark, weakly interacting nature. Existing approaches rely on patterned driving, local control, or structured environments. We propose a platform-independent protocol based on projective measurements on a single TLE. For permutation-symmetric ensembles, a single measurement yields appreciable occupation of single-excitation subradiant steady states. For generic arrays, repeated measurements on one emitter drive the unmeasured TLEs into a nearly pure state with large overlap with the subradiant Dicke subspace.

AI.tldr: Protocol using projective measurements on a single two-level emitter to prepare subradiant steady states in collectively emitting quantum systems
AI.motivation: Subradiant steady states of collectively emitting quantum two-level emitters are difficult to prepare due to their dark, weakly interacting nature, and existing approaches require complex patterned driving, local control, or structured environments.
AI.method: Propose a platform-independent protocol based on projective measurements on a single two-level emitter. For permutation-symmetric ensembles, a single measurement yields appreciable occupation of single-excitation subradiant steady states. For generic arrays, repeated measurements on one emitter drive the unmeasured emitters into a nearly pure state with large overlap with the subradiant Dicke subspace.
AI.result: The protocol enables preparation of subradiant steady states without requiring complex control schemes, with single measurements sufficient for symmetric ensembles and repeated measurements effective for generic arrays.
AI.conclusion: Projective measurements on a single emitter provide a simple, platform-independent approach to preparing subradiant steady states in collectively emitting quantum systems, overcoming the challenges posed by their dark, weakly interacting nature.

title: Nonlocal prediction of quantum measurement outcomes
summary: We define nonlocal predictability as how well one observer can predict another's measurement outcomes without classical communication, given full knowledge of the shared quantum state and measurement settings. The local bound on nonlocal predictability is defined as the maximum probability with which one observer can correctly predict the other's measurement outcome prior to measurement. We show that product states always meet this bound, while all pure entangled states and some classically correlated states can exceed it. This demonstrates a nonlocal phenomenon since the predictability of measurement outcomes increases after the measurement. Perfect nonlocal predictability for arbitrary projective measurements occurs only for maximally entangled states among all pure states, underscoring their special role. Comparing pure entangled states with their dephased versions, we find that dephasing on one subsystem can enhance nonlocal predictability for a broad class of states and measurements - a counterintuitive, noise-induced advantage that vanishes for maximally entangled states under any projective measurement.
